#121176. Three Ways Families Can Make Mental Health Problems Worse

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (903 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Three Ways Families Can Make Mental Health Problems Worse

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 1959, a sociologist named George Brown led a study of 156 men diagnosed with schizophrenia who had recently been discharged.
  • According to recent reports, more studies followed.
  • A 1989 study highlighted that the single best predictor of relapse among patients who’d been hospitalized for depression was their response to the question, “How critical is your spouse of you?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recent findings suggest that in 1959, a sociologist named George Brown led a study of 156 men diagnosed with schizophrenia who had recently been discharged. Most went to live with family members: parents, spouses, siblings. A smaller group lived alone in rented rooms. Brown followed them for a year. He found that among those who lived with family, about one-third ended up in the hospital. Of those who lived alone, none did.

According to recent reports, more studies followed. Data from a 1976 study suggested that cutting back on time with a critical relative was roughly as protective as antipsychotic medication against relapse in schizophrenia.

A 1989 study highlighted that the single best predictor of relapse among patients who’d been hospitalized for depression was their response to the question, “How critical is your spouse of you?”.

A 1998 meta-analysis found that a critical or overinvolved family was linked to poor outcomes for conditions as diverse as depression, bipolar disorder, and eating disorders.

Recent findings suggest that what’s interesting is that these aren’t families you’d ordinarily deem “abusive.” The standard framework for assessing family dysfunction today, the adverse childhood experiences framework, doesn’t capture them. These studies examine lesser forms of dysfunction, what many of us would call “normal.”.

Industry observers note that I’m going to wager that you’ve never heard of this body of research. As a historian, I find that this raises an equally fascinating question: Why not?

In the 1960s, psychiatrists were quick to blame parents for mental illness, especially mothers. Schizophrenia was explained by a “schizophrenogenic mother,” autism by a “refrigerator mother.” But the more careful psychiatrists emphasized that the problem was never solely the mother, or solely the father, but the family dynamic that engulfed mother, father, and child.

Recent findings suggest that by the late 1970s, however, parents of patients were tired of being told that their kids’ mental illness was their fault. This era led to the emergence of groups like the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill, founded in 1979 by two Wisconsin mothers whose sons had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

It has been revealed that such groups promoted the emerging biological perspective that viewed mental illnesses as brain disorders. Historian Anne Harrington, in Mind Fixers (2019), documents the role such advocacy groups played in popularizing the biomedical view.

By the 1990s, the biomedical model was firmly established in the American psyche. Everything was now a chemical imbalance. Family dynamics seemed to be off the table for good.

Industry observers note that today, psychiatrists claim that they’ve moved away from narrow biological reductionism to accept a “biopsychosocial” model, one that explores the whole range of factors that create and sustain mental illness. You’d think the family would have been put back on the map. It wasn’t, with one partial exception.

Advocates of the biopsychosocial framework often use the adverse childhood experiences framework to assess family precursors to mental illness. But its entries center on extreme forms of trauma, abuse, and neglect. The lesser forms of family dysfunction that psychiatrists once sought to understand remain largely off the table.

To my knowledge, only one research tradition has kept the family in view from the 1950s to today: “expressed emotion” research. It has built a robust body of findings.

Its core finding, put at the most general level, is that high “expressed emotion” in families is a strong predictor of relapse in numerous illnesses, including schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, and eating disorders. To break it down a bit more:.

According to recent reports, 1. Criticism: When the family member expresses constant disapproval, or when they insinuate that the person is lazy or selfish.

2. Hostility: When the family member disparages the person for who they are, or when they believe that the person could “snap out of it.”.

In a recent development, 3. Emotional overinvolvement: When the family shows excessive concern for the person’s well-being, and when they convey the message that the person is “unable to cope” with the world.

A 1994 analysis of 25 studies, covering more than 1,300 patients around the world, found that the link between expressed emotion and relapse was “overwhelming.” More recent work, by researchers such as Preethi Premkumar, has extended these findings to people who have never been diagnosed with anything, showing that young adults with mild psychosis-like traits (“schizotypy”) see their relatives as more critical, and the feeling of being criticized goes along with depression and anger.

Industry observers note that as I know from my own experience, having a loved one with schizophrenia or other serious mental disorder can be overwhelming, taxing, and uncertain. It can create a mix of intense feelings like pity, guilt, and anger.

Proponents of expressed emotion research emphasize that the solution isn’t to lay more shame and blame on families, but counseling and education. Clinical practice guidelines universally recommend family counseling.

Can families cause mental illness? The jury’s still out. But they can sustain mental health crises and make them more likely to recur. That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t go home for the holidays. But it may help to be aware of how family dynamics can affect your mental health.

Tesla launches FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.
  • According to recent reports, tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a new live visualization that looks seriously impressive.
  • Tesla announced the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.

According to recent reports, tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a new live visualization that looks seriously impressive. If the driving improvements are as real as the visuals, this is a substantial enhancement.

Tesla announced the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes. The manufacturer didn’t say which vehicles get it first, but it has previously told investors that its AI4 (HW4) computer is enough to run v15.

Here are Tesla’s release notes for FSD v15:.

v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. Includes:.

Tesla’s main announcement also says FSD can now slow down for speed cameras, and it adds Bike Rack Mode, which allows FSD with a bike rack or a similar hitch accessory. Navigation learning only covers the start and end of trips for now; Tesla says later v15 releases will expand it to the entire route.

Sources indicate that the new visualization is the flashiest part, and based on the video Tesla shared, it’s super impressive. The center screen indicates a detailed, rendered version of the street around the car, far beyond the current FSD visualization.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW.

In a recent development, tesla calls it “Reality View” in its announcement and “Tesla Augmented Reality” in the release notes. The notes say it replaces all the separate model signals with a single end-to-end visualization that uses less compute, and Tesla says it lets the driver “see & control what FSD is planning to do.” If that works as advertised, it could make supervising the system a lot easier.

Industry observers note that what stands out more is where Tesla is focusing. Almost every driving improvement in the release notes targets an area where FSD struggles today.

In a recent development, signs are a big one. In a test published in September, Brussels nonprofit Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it drove through, averaging 44 km/h. In most of those zones, the car’s screen demonstrated a 50 km/h limit. It didn’t read the sign.

Potholes are another. In August, Musk remarked pothole avoidance was “coming soon”, something he had already promised back in 2019. Today, FSD still drives straight through them.

School zones are on the list too. NHTSA is reviewing a petition claiming Tesla’s Robotaxis speed through active school zones, on top of an investigation it opened in October 2025 into FSD traffic-law violations like running red lights. Slowing for speed cameras fits the same theme, though it also suggests Tesla is fine with FSD going over the limit when there’s no camera around.

Recent findings suggest that so if v15 really fixes these, it’s a very good update. The question is by how much.

In a recent development, one change goes the other way. Tesla says it is “decreasing strictness” of driver monitoring in higher-speed driver profiles, at a time when sleeping drivers on FSD keep making headlines and Tesla is tightening monitoring in Europe at regulators’ request.

In a recent development, the release notes clear up what the “25x” refers to: Tesla says the new vision encoder improves the critical intervention rate by 25x. That’s the right metric to measure progress toward unsupervised driving. But Tesla still doesn’t share the actual number, only the multiplier.

The math gets interesting fast. Our data from earlier this year suggested FSD v14 could go a couple thousand miles between critical interventions. A 25x improvement on that would put v15 around 50,000 miles between critical interventions, well beyond the roughly 10,000 miles we’ve said Tesla needs for a limited unsupervised service. If that were true across the fleet, we could see Tesla having its most meaningful push toward autonomy in a long time.

And v15 already carries plenty of hype. In April, Elon Musk wrote that v15 “will far exceed human levels of safety, even in completely unsupervised and complex situations.” We pointed out at the time that he had said similar things about v12 and v14. In August, Tesla told JPMorgan that v15 is a “step-change” built on seven “core technologies,” with about 40% of them already running in its Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

Recent findings suggest that FSD has never improved in a straight line. Every major version has brought real gains along with latest problems, and point releases regularly go backward.

It has been revealed that when v14 arrived in October 2025, it came with hallucinations, brake stabbing, and excessive speeding, and early crowdsourced data highlighted about 732 miles between critical disengagements, below what we expected. It then improved a lot. Then the v14.2 updates went backward before Musk sold v14.3 as the version where “the last big piece of the puzzle finally lands.”.

Seven months and a long string of point releases later, owners are still supervising, and Tesla now needs v15 to deliver what v14.3 was supposed to.

I remain skeptic of Tesla's autonomous driving until they apply for the California DMV permit to begin testing autonomous driving without a driver. California is a major enough of a potential market for robotaxi that Tesla is operating a human driver taxi service. The common presumption is that Tesla is avoiding California autonomous testing because it requires disclosing critical interventions and other data which wouldn't be favorable to Tesla's claims.

According to recent reports, the visuals are super impressive. That much we can already judge from the video, and Reality View could make FSD easier to understand and supervise.

In a recent development, the driving side is harder to judge. Tesla is going straight at the weaknesses that owners and regulators complain about most: misread speed limits, potholes, school zones, debris. If v15 delivers real progress on all of those, it’s a really good update.

Industry observers note that but “improved detection” doesn’t tell us how much better, and a 25x multiplier without the underlying number is hard to check. FSD has gone two steps forward, one step back throughout its history, with point releases regularly breaking things the previous version handled fine. And Tesla still won’t publish the disengagement data that would settle it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that cop Brian O’Connor infiltrates the L.A.
  • Now a fugitive with a Nissan Skyline but no visible means of support, Brian joins the feds to catch a drug lord who tortures a corrupt cop with the ol’ rat-in-the-ice-bucket trick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if the Fast & Furious franchise taught us anything, it’s that there’s always another gear, and there’s no such thing as a bad plot­line. (Also: family.) To honor its silver anniversary, here’s a recap of the F&F universe, as it expanded from the L.A. street-racing scene to encompass every action-film trope, device, and format ever scrawled on a Hollywood studio whiteboard.

The Fast and the Furious (2001).

Industry observers note that cop Brian O’Connor infiltrates the L.A. import-car scene to bust hijackers who steal DVD players and at least one sweet 13-inch TV/VCR combo. He bonds with bald kingpin Dominic Toretto, then lets him go. Executives smell a sequel. Toretto has other plans: The Chronicles of Riddick. Danger to manifold: 10/10.

Now a fugitive with a Nissan Skyline but no visible means of support, Brian joins the feds to catch a drug lord who tortures a corrupt cop with the ol’ rat-in-the-ice-bucket trick. Roman Pearce replaces Dom as the bald guy at the emotional core. Camaro jumps onto yacht. Danger to manifold: 5/10.

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006).

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006).

Brian who? Now it’s Sean, a high schooler who looks like he’s 35. Busted for street racing, he’s sent to Tokyo, the capital of street racing. He crosses the yakuza-­connected Drift King and falls in with Han Seoul-­Oh, who can’t stop snacking. Dom cameo as sequel bait. Danger to manifold: 七/10.

Industry observers note that dom’s back, and the crew now executes road-train robberies in the Dominican Republic. Brian, now FBI, infiltrates a heroin pipeline. Letty dies. Dom seeks vengeance. A Road Warrior–style chase ends in a killer wheelie, literally. Dom is busted, but a sequel is nigh. Danger to manifold: 3/10.

Street racing? Nah. We’re a heist franchise, dog. Dom’s crew, now fully Hollywood four-quadrant tested, steals a crime lord’s fortune in Brazil. A former wrestler highlights up as DSS agent Luke Hobbs. Bald jokes and legal ambiguity ensue. Everybody walks with $100 million. Danger to manifold: 1.5/10.

Hobbs is back, and we meet British scoundrel number one, Owen Shaw, an ex-SAS mercenary who drives a ramp car that flips police cruisers like a spatula. Letty is alive (huh?), with amnesia, and on Shaw’s payroll. Gisele dies. (Who’s Gisele again?) Danger to manifold: –10/10.

Jason Statham (really?) is Deckard Shaw, Owen’s scoundrel brother, who fireballs Dom’s family home. The crew parachutes into Azerbaijan in their cars. A Lykan HyperSport jumps between three Abu Dhabi office towers. Han’s dead (like we believe that). The saddest ending imaginable. Danger to manifold: N/A.

Fate, F9, Fast X, Hobbs & Shaw (2017–23).

Roll call: John Cena. Dame Helen Mirren. Charlize Theron. Jason Momoa. Sir Idris Elba. Old villains are in the crew now. We’re in Cuba (thanks, Obama), Antarctica, a sub­marine, and a Pontiac Fiero in space. Han? Gisele? Both alive. It’s just a parody of action movies now, right? Danger to manifold: $7 billion/10.

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • According to recent reports, sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals upcoming insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but new research challenges this conclusion.

According to recent reports, sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals upcoming insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich said in a statement.

In a recent development, the pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

“There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” remarked Schultrich.

Double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s currently clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

In a recent development, the same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

Industry observers note that “It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.

#121170. Breaking: Think Someone Envies You? Here’s Why You Might Be Wrong

Breaking: Think Someone Envies You? Here’s Why You Might Be Wrong

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • As the holidays approach, you're likely to meet fresh people and socialize with colleagues and family you don't normally see the rest of the year.
  • In such settings, you're also more likely to come into situations where you sense a bit of "healthy competition." Turkey Trot, anyone?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As the holidays approach, you're likely to meet fresh people and socialize with colleagues and family you don't normally see the rest of the year.

In such settings, you're also more likely to come into situations where you sense a bit of "healthy competition." Turkey Trot, anyone? You may also interact with people playing the "one-up" game, where someone shares a more intense version of the story or situation you just shared.

Whenever people gather, we're assessing and comparing. Everyone does it. It's natural. It helps us understand how we fit in and get cues on how to behave.

Envy not only can occur, but it can also help you navigate these times...though not in the way most people expect.

When some people discover I've written a book on envy, but they are not yet aware of its contents, they will tell me, "I don't feel envy, but I know a lot of people who do." They will then proceed to tell me about the people who envy them.

According to recent reports, they don't know that I believe that everyone envies. It is a universal emotion. Unpleasant, yes, but not necessarily a harmful one.

It has been revealed that I get it. In this culture where envy is often seen as a deadly sin, it's hard to admit feeling envy.

It has been revealed that but not acknowledging one's own envy is unfortunate because you miss out on all that envy can reveal to you. However, that isn't the mistake I want to focus on here. I believe the bigger mistake is to assume that you know when someone else is feeling envy.

Recent findings suggest that first, we can't be certain it is envy they are feeling. Not only is it impossible to read minds, but we also can't reliably detect envy from their faces. As envy researcher Jens Lange told me, "If there were [a unique envy facial expression], we would likely suppress it.".

Sources indicate that second, when we ascribe envy to someone else, we create an artificial barrier. We make a negative judgment about their character and lower their status to elevate ourselves. Not even conscious of this, we begin to operate on the false assumption and the distance we've created. It subtly impacts our interactions and our behaviors.

In a recent development, first, adopt a curious mindset. It's harder to stop your mind from thinking of something than it is to suggest something latest to consider. So, instead of saying, "Don't judge or make assumptions," try, "I don't know their story." Remind yourself that you don't know what happened in their past, what just happened moments ago, what their circumstances are, or what their mood is.

Industry observers note that second, dial up the warmth. Amy Cuddy, Susan Fiske, and Peter Glick's research revealed that when people encounter one another, they ask two questions: "Does this person want to harm or help me?" and "Is this person capable of following through with their threat or assistance?" They found that people tend to be envied when they are not warm but competent. So, if it is true that you're envied, more reason to approach with warmth.

During your year-end holiday festivities, try combining these two concepts and adopt a "warm curiosity.".

You may walk away learning unexpected reasons why you like someone you didn't before.

Alicke, M. D., & Zell, E. (2008). Social Comparison and Envy. In R. Smith (Ed.), Envy: Theory and Research (pp. 73–93). Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195327953.003.0005.

Cuddy, A. J. C., Glick, P., & Beninger, A. (2011). The dynamics of warmth and competence judgments, and their outcomes in organizations. Research in Organizational Behavior, 31, 73–98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.riob.2011.10.004.

Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification.
  • UPDATE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.
  • “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!

UPDATE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.

“An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura. “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”.

Pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any newly introduced ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.

Recent findings suggest that when you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety, what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance. It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.

A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.

Country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer.

Sources indicate that what’s more, a newly introduced wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford, Slate, and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house.

Industry observers note that with only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging, public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is.

It has been revealed that unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs (if there even are any) to a minimum.

Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.

In a recent development, if disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators, freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days, either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.

If you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days, that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.

It’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a new pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals, new tax incentives, and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model.

As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.

Industry observers note that at the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians. Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.

Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.

Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power, you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers.

In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs.

We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer, along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles.

In a recent development, and while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some upcoming, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.

There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility company to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

In a recent development, that remarked, it’s been a long time since I was back in Ohio, so maybe I’ve forgotten what it’s like. You guys are smart, head on down to the comments and let me know what I missed!

#121168. Breaking: U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1332 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.
  • Industry observers note that the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S.
  • “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, said in a media briefing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.

Industry observers note that the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S. for more than 12 months. On November 17, PAHO revealed the end of the country’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.

“Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, said in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.”.

PAHO’s review examined measles spread starting January 20, 2025, when the first person became ill in a large West Texas outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a recent development, CDC data show 5,412 confirmed measles cases this year as of November 12. That’s the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2025 count of 2,289 cases.

Andi Shane, MD, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, called the U.S. losing measles elimination status “a public health alarm that we are not being effective and we’re not controlling measles as well.”.

The measles virus is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can catch it in a room up to two hours after an infected person has left, according to the CDC.

“There’s really been very little measles in the United States over the past 25 years until January 2025,” William Moss, MD, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healthline.

Losing the status itself doesn’t change much about daily life for most Americans, Moss said. The concern is the measles outbreaks, hospitalizations and deaths behind the loss, he said.

He called the loss “a massive red flag” after “enormous efforts over the past 26 years” to keep the status.

Recent findings suggest that A country loses its elimination status when there is “uninterrupted circulation of the same virus genotype and lineage for 12 months or more,” according to PAHO. Shane explained it this way: “For the past 12 months in the United States, we’ve had ongoing circulation of the measles virus and person-to-person transmission is occurring.”.

Canada lost its elimination status in November 2025, and the U.K. and five European countries lost theirs earlier in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. can regain the status. “Other countries have done that,” Moss noted. Brazil, which lost its status in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Venezuela, which lost its status in 2018, regained it in 2023, according to PAHO.

Sources indicate that before the measles vaccine, measles infected an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans each year, according to the CDC. Among reported cases, about 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 needed hospital care, and 1,000 developed encephalitis, or brain swelling.

Here’s a timeline of measles elimination in the U.S.:.

In a recent development, moss stated elimination efforts “really intensified” after a large outbreak from 1989 to 1992. Part of that push was “really promoting school entry vaccination checks,” he said.

“That was one of the key policy changes that I think allowed for measles elimination in the United States.”.

Every state and Washington, D.C., require children to be vaccinated against measles to attend school, though exemptions vary by state, according to the nonprofit health policy organization KFF.

Fewer kindergartners are getting the MMR vaccine, according to the CDC.

Recent findings suggest that kindergarten MMR coverage fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. About 280,000 kindergartners started the 2025–2026 school year without records showing they had completed the MMR series, the CDC reported.

Shane said “95 out of 100 people need to be protected against measles” for a community to get herd protection.

“So since we’ve been below that for many, many months, that is also contributing to the loss of our elimination status,” she remarked.

“It takes two things to have a measles outbreak,” Moss said. A community needs low vaccine coverage, and someone with measles has to enter it and “start the chain of transmission,” he said.

About 96% of this year’s cases were among people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, up from 93% in 2025, according to the CDC.

Moss stated many of those cases are adults.

According to recent reports, “This is particularly true in Pennsylvania, where about two-thirds of the cases are in adults,” he remarked. Many never got vaccinated as kids and grew up while measles was rare, so they never built natural immunity, he said.

He noted that having so many unvaccinated adults puts pregnant people and adults with chronic conditions like lung disease at risk of serious illness. The U.S. has already seen “dozens of pregnant women actually getting infected during pregnancy,” he remarked.Infected parents can also spread measles to young children and grandparents, Shane said. Shane traced much of the hesitancy to the pandemic. “With COVID there’s been an overall distrust in vaccines and vaccination that initially started with COVID but has now spread to other vaccines,” she said.

Moss pointed to the federal government. “We know what it takes to achieve and sustain elimination. We have the expertise. We have the resources,” he said.

In a recent development, he cited staff cuts at the CDC and noted messaging from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Donald Trump has undermined vaccine confidence. He called federal messaging on vaccines “really mixed and weak.”.

Moss also criticized the President’s August 10 executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split into separate shots for each disease.

“There’s no justification for that, and those vaccines don’t even exist in the United States,” he said.

Industry observers note that measles may cause ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia, encephalitis and, in some cases, death, according to the CDC. The disease may also weaken the immune system for weeks to a year after recovery, raising the risk of flu, COVID-19, or RSV, Shane remarked. “It’s not a benign childhood disease,” Moss said.

The best protection against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine, which are about 97% effective, according to the CDC. Shane stated, “There are not very many other things we do in life that give you such great protection.” People who missed doses can still catch up, she added. “If you just don’t know or can’t tell, there’s no harm — as long as you’re eligible — in getting another MMR vaccine.”.

Shane added that “parents really want to do the right thing for their children.”.

According to recent reports, “We know that the MMR vaccine — that’s the vaccine that provides protection against measles — is a safe vaccine. It’s a very effective vaccine,” Shane said.

Babies under 12 months are too young for the vaccine. “So they depend on the protection of the people around them,” Shane stated.

The CDC recommends a first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at 4 to 6 years. Babies 6 to 11 months old who will travel internationally should get an early dose, and adults without proof of immunity should get at least one dose, according to the CDC.

Recent findings suggest that to stop the outbreaks, Moss noted the U.S. will need to “increase vaccine coverage, particularly in those communities that have had long-standing low vaccine rates.”.

So far, the response has been “more reactive than proactive,” Moss remarked. Public health teams scramble once an outbreak starts, he said, and he wants more outreach to at-risk communities before measles arrives.

“I am worried about the ability of the United States to regain measles elimination status in the current climate,” Moss said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season.
  • According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.
  • Industry observers note that short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season. United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) volunteer and photographer Dan Rapp spotted the egg on George and Geraldine’s nest this weekend. The pair are endangered short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian, and this is their 10th straight year together.

According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.

Industry observers note that short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill. The monogamous birds can live up to 50 years, and nest on islands and atolls where they typically lay one egg per season. Short-tailed albatrosses are listed as endangered, and biologists estimate that there are only 10,000 left in the wild.

George and Geraldine were banded as chicks on Torishima Island, Japan. They raised their first chick together during the 2018–2019 breeding season. The duo is the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, but other members of their species were observed last season. After spending the summer/non-nesting season apart, George was first spotted at Midway Atoll on October 18. He was reunited with Geraldine by October 22.

This remote group of islands sit about 1,250 miles from Hawaii’s capital Honolulu and are most famous for a pivotal World War II battle. Every fall, it becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species. Some notable albatross species are the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species and the Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis). At over 70 years old, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird. She has produced roughly 50 to 60 eggs, and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime, and she became a grandmother once again in March. Wisdom has not been spotted yet this nesting season.

Bird enthusiasts from around the world can eavesdrop on this albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates. Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch fluffy albatross chicks.

Audi Files Patent Application for Physical Buttons That Fold Out From Behind a Touchscreen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical buttons have a lot going for them.
  • Sources indicate that as CarMoses first discovered, Audi has filed for a patent application that describes a motorized switch bar, which pivots out from behind the display’s lower edge.
  • For those who do want the physical buttons, there are plenty of reasons to get excited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical buttons have a lot going for them. They’re easy to find by feel, satisfying to use, and generally pretty good at staying wherever the automaker installed them. Well, it seems Audi has an idea that would change that last part: it involves hiding the buttons behind a touchscreen, then deploying them when needed.

Sources indicate that as CarMoses first discovered, Audi has filed for a patent application that describes a motorized switch bar, which pivots out from behind the display’s lower edge. The screen stays fixed, while the physical controls swing into position beneath it. Interestingly, when stowed, the bar apparently has an on-screen counterpart with the same functions lined up in the same order, so those who don't want physical buttons can avoid them entirely.

For those who do want the physical buttons, there are plenty of reasons to get excited. First, Audi states in its patent documents with the German government that the switches can deploy at startup, via voice controls, or via gestures. Moving the controls from the screen to the physical switches also provides more total screen room for people. (In one example, the physical bar deploys when a movie opens, leaving more room for the video.).

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, this could be a great way to meet the demands of more people. Designers love a clean dashboard without physical buttons and switches. Plenty of drivers really love having that switchgear. This system allows owners to pick whatever they want on the fly.

According to recent reports, the timing makes plenty of sense too. Audi has openly remarked that it views moving toward more mechanical controls as the right direction. Of course, adding extra complexity to the once-simple idea of buttons also can increase the cost down the line when it comes time for repairs, but even so, this idea is certainly a fascinating solution to a very modern problem.

But why wait for the Scion to get here? Right now, there’s a legally imported keijidosha pickup over at Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos): a 2000 Daihatsu HiJet, which happens to be the same model on which the new Scion is based.

Over there, these little pickups work just as hard as larger trucks, carrying a little less cargo but doing the work of road repair, smaller construction projects, plumbing work, and, of course, gardening. For the latter, there's even an annual competition to put together the best bonsai garden in a kei truck bed.

On this side of the Pacific, you'll need to carefully check what your state laws say about the use of kei trucks on public roads, as some states allow them to be driven on roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less, while others only allow them to be used on private property.

Even with those restrictions, this HiJet would be incredibly useful for ferrying around livestock feed on a farm, or shuttling small deliveries around a busy factory complex, or even getting evil minions around a hollowed-out volcano lair. If it does pass muster for on-road use where you live, these trucks are surprisingly plucky to drive, and would make for the ultimate DIY partner. Plenty of hunters and fishermen also appreciate four-wheel-drive kei trucks for their ability to squeeze down narrow tracks where full-size pickups can't go.

The bed is also surprisingly flexible, with fold-down sides that transform it into a mini-flatbed truck. The payload is stouter than you'd think, rated for 770 pounds, so though it may be tiny, it's still mighty.

It has been revealed that daihatsu has plenty of experience building kei trucks and cars, including as a subcontractor for other companies, including Toyota. The HiJet has been around since the 1960s, making it Japan's version of the F-150.

Motive power comes from a 659cc three-cylinder engine plonked in the middle of the chassis, good for a whopping 42 horsepower. That power goes to the rear wheels through a five-speed manual transmission, or you can hit a button and get power to all four corners. The selling dealer has recently replaced the battery and done a mild tune-up, including fresh spark plugs and an oil change.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a red wave of Chinese-built electric vehicles breaks over Europe and Canada, Xiaomi is selling its electric cars outside of China for the first time ever – and its starting its push for global growth with the UAE in 2027.

Xiaomi is selling its electrified vehicles to buyers outside of China for first time this week, with the SU7 sedan, YU7 crossover, and Skynomad SUV now listed for sale throughout the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The manufacturer isn’t going it alone, however.

Xiomi is working local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive, rather than operating its own retail network, with Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun confirming that the firm would officially enter Western car markets next year at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen held 17NOV.

CarNewsChina reports that Gargash Prime Automotive is offering 13 variants across the Xiaomi SU7 sedan, YU7 SUV, and Skynomad extended-range electric SUV lineup, with retail prices starting at 169,900 AED ($~46,200 US) for the SU7 Standard and climbing all the way up to 375,900 AED ($~102,000 US) for the range-topping SU7 Ultra.

Not to lump a bunch of nations with their own rich heritage and car culture together, but it’s fair to say that drivers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait love their supercars – and the brand’s Xiaomi SU7 Ultra might be one of the most super of them all, thanks to fully 1,548 hp from three high-torque electric motors, the SU7 Ultra can sprint from 0-100 km/h (62 mph) in under two seconds on its way to a towering, 217 mph top speed.

In a recent development, it’s not just a straight-line speed machine, either. Xiaomi gave its go-fast flagship a serious track-focused makeover on its way to becomig the “Utlra,” complete with carbon-ceramic brakes, an aggressive (if controversial) composite aero package, an enormous rear wing, and a chassis tuned to tackle the turns the Green Hell of the Nürburgring.

And, at a relatively reasonable $102,000 equivalent price, I’d be willing to bet that a lot of the hypercar-loving Emiratis will be eager to get their hands on one.

The first customer deliveries of the Xiaomi SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard, and Skynomad N70 Pro models are scheduled for December of this year, with deliveries of the remaining variants scheduled for February 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, THE IDEA OF "newly introduced" television demonstrates is a little bit of a tricky one these days.
  • It has been revealed that but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong.
  • Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something upcoming, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, THE IDEA OF "newly introduced" television demonstrates is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

It has been revealed that but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something upcoming, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

Sources indicate that and they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Sources indicate that netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO).

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock).

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

It has been revealed that one of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

Sources indicate that this wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The fresh season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the massive and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

In a recent development, the erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting upcoming shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

Sources indicate that from the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

Sources indicate that there are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

Industry observers note that this series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in indicates like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those aims have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

Jury Duty: Firm Retreat (Prime Video).

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

According to recent reports, riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix).

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

Wasps recognize faces—and it keeps them from killing each other

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, wasps can recognize faces.
  • “These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan, a study co-author and neuroethologist  at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, remarked in a statement.
  • Sources indicate that the team studied the northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscates).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wasps can recognize faces. But don’t worry. They may not be telling human faces apart the way that cows can. The stingy insects tell their nestmates apart by recognizing different color patterns on their faces, so they know the difference between mama wasp and papa wasp or a friend versus a foe. A study published today in the journal Cell details how they use specialized brain cells to pull this off.

“These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan, a study co-author and neuroethologist  at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, remarked in a statement. “These groups of neurons are all firing, and each neuron has a slightly different preference for one face or another.”.

Sources indicate that the team studied the northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscates). These roughly half-inch long bugs are found from southern parts of Canada through Florida and Texas. Their name comes from the paper-like nests made of hexagonal cells that they often construct under building eaves and on the ceilings of porches. Paper wasps also have silk that shine under UV light, giving these nests a secretive fluorescent glow.

Female northern paper wasps use facial recognition to remember another wasp’s place in the nest’s hierarchy. Once this hierarchy is established, recognizing faces helps maintain social order, without a constant battle for dominance.

In a recent development, wasps may be using a method for facial recognition that’s similar to how primates (including humans) tell faces apart, even though both methods evolved independently. Even with brains about the size of a single rice grain, Jernigan said that wasps are “able to do this incredibly complex task of remembering and recalling individuals.” They do this by spotting the differences between the color patterns on one wasp face versus another, with the help of specialized neurons.

Wasps can also perform something called social eavesdropping. When two wasps fight to establish dominance in the nest hierarchy, one wasps can watch the two unknown wasps quarrel. Once that spectator wasp sees one of them, it will know whether or not it needs to fight for dominance.

Industry observers note that “They will treat the winner of that fight independently in a third interaction differently than they would the loser,” Jernigan explained. “Despite having these small brains and relatively simple vision, they have these really complex social lives that revolve around this specialized ability to recognize each other.”.

According to the team, understanding this facial recognition could help us understand human brain systems as well.

In a recent development, “This system, hopefully, holds the potential to help us understand our own brains as we study the circuit connections and the role of experience in giving rise to identity recognition,” Jernigan said. “It’s really remarkable that they have this kind of really human-like or primate-like ability that you wouldn’t typically expect for an insect. And I think it’s almost unbelievable that they have some of the similar kind of neural computations for doing a similar task as we do. It takes a tremendous amount of neural connections to do something similar in a primate.”.

#121161. Breaking: Does Black Friday Make Everything Else Seem Expensive?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (849 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Does Black Friday Make Everything Else Seem Expensive?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Industry observers note that there is something rather irritating about seeing a product heavily discounted during the Black Friday sales, only to see it back at full price a few days later.
  • Industry observers note that black Friday discounts might do more than encourage us to spend money during the sales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Industry observers note that there is something rather irritating about seeing a product heavily discounted during the Black Friday sales, only to see it back at full price a few days later. Before the sale, the original price might have seemed perfectly reasonable. But once the excitement of the sale has died down, it feels expensive, and paying the full price seems almost painful.

Industry observers note that black Friday discounts might do more than encourage us to spend money during the sales. They could also change our perception of value and how much we're willing to pay for things long after the bargains have disappeared.

When we buy something, we tend to think that we're making a rational judgment about whether it's worth the price. But how do we decide what something is actually worth?

According to recent reports, one way is by comparing the asking price with what we've paid before or what we've seen the product selling for elsewhere. This gives us what is known as a reference price, a sort of benchmark we use to decide whether something seems expensive or cheap.

It has been revealed that over time, and after many repeated purchases, we become accustomed to paying a certain amount for a particular product. We accept that amount as its normal price, and it becomes what we expect to pay. But then Black Friday happens, which nowadays may last for a full month rather than one day, and that same product is suddenly available for considerably less.

Sources indicate that even though we know perfectly well that the discount is temporary, that lower price starts to influence what we think the product should cost. It can become a fresh reference point against which we judge future prices.

It has been revealed that when the sale ends and the price returns to normal, the amount we have become used to paying no longer seems quite so reasonable. The deal has changed our perception of value.

When a discount changes what we think something is worth, it can also change whether we're willing to buy it at all.

Recent findings suggest that across three studies, Guo (2026) found that consumers who had seen an extremely low price were less willing to buy the same product later at a higher price than those who had seen a smaller discount. What was interesting was why they didn't want to buy it.

Seeing the lower price reduced how much participants thought the product was worth. The prospect of paying the higher price also increased their anticipated regret. They expected to feel worse about buying something they knew had previously been priced for considerably less.

It has been revealed that it didn't matter whether participants had previously bought the product at the cheaper price. Simply knowing it had once been available for less was enough to discourage a future purchase. We don't necessarily have to miss out on a bargain for it to change our perception of value, which the researcher called the postdiscount effect.

The findings raise an interesting question about Black Friday. If retailers spend weeks convincing us that their products are worth buying at heavily discounted prices, what happens when they expect us to start paying full price again?

This is where Black Friday might become a problem for retailers themselves. Black Friday is designed to encourage us to buy more by making products temporarily cheaper. But in doing so, retailers may also be changing what we're willing to pay for those products in the future. They could be inadvertently teaching us that their products are worth less than they originally claimed.

In a recent development, the more accustomed we become to seeing discounts, the more we might begin questioning whether the full price is ever worth paying. Why buy something today when it might be cheaper again next month in the post-Christmas sales? Why pay the normal price when we've seen exactly how little a retailer was prepared to sell it for last week?

There's nothing wrong with taking advantage of a good Black Friday discount. You've made a sensible decision if you've been planning to buy something and find it cheaper. The problem is when we allow that temporary price to determine what we think something should cost long after the sales have finished.

Sources indicate that that's the irony of Black Friday. Retailers spend much of November getting us excited and convincing us that we're going to get extraordinary value for our money. In doing so, they might also be convincing us that their products were never worth the original asking price.

They may have saved us money today, but they've made everything seem more expensive tomorrow.

According to recent reports, guo, T. (2026). From inaction inertia to the postdiscount effect: How a lower price reduces subsequent purchase after it expires. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 39(4), e70092.
