In a recent development, at one point, Top Gear was one of the biggest shows on television of any sort. It has been a long time since the glory days of Clarkson, Hammond, and May, though, and multiple efforts to revive the BBC’s legendary automotive series have failed to come close to the impact of the original. The show has not been in production since its newest episodes aired in 2022, but a upcoming host is about to change that very soon. On Wednesday, the BBC confirmed that celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay is taking over the mantle of Top Gear host starting in 2028. Ramsay will be the first host of the show since production paused after a crash involving then-presenter Freddie Flintoff four years ago.

An announcement from the BBC makes no mention of any potential co-hosts alongside Ramsay, but does add that he will be hosting along with “as yet unnamed co-presenters.” The same announcement quotes BBC Studios Entertainment executive Suzy Lamb as saying that the new Top Gear “won't be a nostalgic reboot" and would instead be a “bold and unmissable new chapter” of the show, lines that suggest a major format change could come with the new host.

While Ramsay is most famous for his career as a chef and host of cooking-related demonstrates, he is also a long-time enthusiast who takes his own cars to the track. He even combined the interests back in 2023, cooking a grilled cheese sandwich in the engine bay of his Aston Martin Valkyrie during a track day. This past weekend, he competed in a celebrity race in Lego Formula 1 cars at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everyone’s going off-roading these days—or at least buying cars that look like they can. Even Bentley, the British automaker synonymous with wealth and high-class style, is reportedly getting in on the off-road action.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, Bentley revealed an off-road concept based on the Bentayga Speed that featured more suspension travel as well as an increased track width and ride height. The Bentley X concept rolled on forged 22-inch wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires. It also debuted at the FAT Ice Race in Austria with over a foot of ground clearance, partnership decals lining the sides and hood, spotlights, and a roof-mounted go-kart.

See all results for new 2027 Bentley Bentayga for sale near 20817.

According to recent reports, bentley CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser said public response to the X concept was “really surprisingly positive” in a recent interview with Automotive News. He added that a production Bentayga based on the X concept is “on the horizon,” though nothing is finalized yet.

The current Bentayga is approaching its 10th year on the market, still in its first generation. Walliser also said the luxury SUV is due for a redesign, though it’s still too early for details. However, he confirmed the Bentayga is here to stay as the larger, gas-powered counterpart to the electric Torcal SUV, which is set to hit the market for the 2028 model year and will occupy a similar segment as the Bentayga.

Industry observers note that as with most concepts, the production version of the off-road Bentayga will probably be much less flashy than the X concept—and most definitely won’t come with a go-kart. But knobby tires, a taller ride height, and more exterior lighting would be plausible in a production variant. Paired with the Bentayga Speed’s 641-hp twin-turbo V-8, a grittier version would be a notable addition to the off-road luxury SUV landscape.

EU pushes back Tesla ‘Full Self-Driving’ vote meeting again, now set for December 15

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned.
  • A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the latest date to Reuters.
  • But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned. The meeting is now December 15.

A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the latest date to Reuters. The Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) has already discussed Tesla’s file at two meetings without putting it to a vote.

Two weeks isn’t much on its own. But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.

Industry observers note that in late 2025, Tesla told owners the Dutch regulator RDW had “committed” to approving FSD in February 2026. The RDW publicly corrected it. The Dutch approval came on April 10. Tesla then pointed owners to an EU-wide vote on October 6, and the TCMV agenda for that meeting had no vote on it.

Industry observers note that even the fresh date took a minute to settle. Belgium’s Flanders transport ministry first said the meeting had moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified it’s December 15. Nobody has given a reason for the change.

And a meeting isn’t a vote. The committee can discuss the file again and push the decision into 2027. Elon Musk mentioned on Tesla’s Q3 call in October that he’d be surprised if EU-wide approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.

EU-wide approval needs at least 15 of the 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU’s population.

Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval so far: the Netherlands, Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, last week, Italy, where Tesla has started the rollout. Using Eurostat population figures, we count those 12 at roughly 29% of the EU’s population.

It has been revealed that germany is the obvious next yes. Berlin got Tesla to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe and then cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in exchange for its support. That would bring the yes camp to about 47%.

Sources indicate that so Tesla still needs France, or both Spain and Poland, to get over 65%. Not a sure thing. Sweden asked the EU in June to reject the system unless Tesla removed the ability to drive above the posted limit at all.

According to recent reports, there’s also a catch for owners. According to Reuters, an EU-level rejection would invalidate the national approvals already granted. If the vote fails, drivers in Italy, the Netherlands, and the 10 other countries who are paying for the system today could lose it.

According to recent reports, A two-week slip in a Brussels committee calendar isn’t too bad, but the delays are adding up. It’s December, the committee has other files, and nothing Reuters reported points to a problem specific to Tesla.

Article and headline should consistently refer to it as Tesla Assisted Driving as that is the name which Tesla has agreed to use in the EU. I think the other big question for EU approval is how easily can the driver avoid paying attention to the road.

Industry observers note that we also don’t think most owners realize what’s at stake. If this vote goes the wrong way, the national approvals go with it. Italian owners who just got the system would lose it a few weeks later.

In a recent development, what would help Tesla’s case more than a fresh name and a lower speed cap is data. The RDW still hasn’t published its test results, and Tesla has never released disengagement data in Europe or anywhere else. Governments on the fence, like Sweden, want to see evidence the system is safe, not a rebrand.

It has been revealed that december 15 is the next date to watch. Does Tesla walk into that room with Germany, France, or Spain on board, or does this slide into 2027?
